---
title: "List Slicing"
unit: 2
cluster: "Working with Lists"
---

We have seen how to select one element of a list by its index. A **slice**
selects several elements at once, such as the first three, the last two, or
every second element. The result is a new list.

In this lesson, we'll learn how to:

* select a range of elements with a slice
* leave out the start or the end of a slice
* use negative indexes in a slice
* select every second element, or reverse a list, with a step

**A slice `[start:stop]` selects the elements from index `start` up to, but not
including, index `stop`.**

## Selecting a range

This list has the twelve months of the year:

```{python}
months = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun",
          "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"]
```

A slice is written with two indexes inside the square brackets, separated by a
colon (`:`). This slice selects the first three months:

```{python}
months[0:3]
```

The element at index `0` is included. The element at index `3`, `"Apr"`, is not.
The stop index is the first element that is left out.

This slice selects the next three months:

```{python}
months[3:6]
```

The number of elements in a slice is `stop - start`. Both slices above have
`3` elements.

The result of a slice is a list, even when it has only one element:

```{python}
months[3:4]
```

## Leaving out the start or the end

When the start index is left out, the slice starts at the beginning of the
list:

```{python}
months[:3]
```

When the stop index is left out, the slice goes to the end of the list:

```{python}
months[9:]
```

## Negative indexes in a slice

A slice can use negative indexes, which count from the end. This slice selects
the last three months:

```{python}
months[-3:]
```

This slice selects everything except the last month:

```{python}
months[:-1]
```

## Slicing command-line arguments

`sys.argv` is a list. Its first element is the script name, and the command-line
arguments come after it. The slice `sys.argv[1:]` selects only the arguments.
Use `%%file` to create `args.py`:

```{python}
%%file args.py
import sys

print(sys.argv[1:])
```

Run it with three arguments:

```{python}
!python args.py one two three
```

The script prints a list of the three arguments, without the script name.

## Slices out of range

An index outside the list produces an `IndexError`. A slice does not. A slice
selects the elements that exist in its range, and ignores the rest:

```{python}
months[10:20]
```

The list has no index `20`, so the slice stops at the end of the list. A slice
that selects nothing produces an empty list:

```{python}
months[20:30]
```

## Taking a step

A slice can have a third number, the **step**. The step is the distance from
one selected element to the next. This slice selects every third month,
starting from the first:

```{python}
months[0:12:3]
```

Start and stop can be left out here too. `months[::3]` selects every third
month from the whole list:

```{python}
months[::3]
```

A negative step goes backwards. A step of `-1` selects every element, from the
end to the start, which gives the list in reverse order:

```{python}
print(months[::-1])
```

The slice does not change `months`. It produces a new list, and `months` keeps
its original order:

```{python}
print(months)
```

The two lists are printed with `print()` because they are too long to display
on one line.

```python
sentence = "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog"
```

```text
First three words: ['the', 'quick', 'brown']
```

## Summary

| Form or rule | Meaning |
|--------------|---------|
| `months[0:3]` | selects the elements at indexes `0`, `1` and `2` |
| `months[start:stop]` | includes index `start` and leaves out index `stop` |
| `months[:3]` | selects the first three elements |
| `months[9:]` | selects the elements from index `9` to the end |
| `months[-3:]` | selects the last three elements |
| `months[:-1]` | selects every element except the last |
| `months[::3]` | selects every third element, starting from the first |
| `months[::-1]` | selects every element in reverse order |
| a slice beyond the end of the list | stops at the end, without an error |
| any slice | produces a new list and leaves the original list unchanged |

And the one idea to carry forward: a slice selects a range of a list and
produces a new list. The start index is included and the stop index is not.
